title: Centesimus Annus (1991)
hookLine: after communism falls: markets have value but also limits

lines: SOME THINGS WEAR A PRICE TAG.
cards: A price tag. Some things wear one easily: a loaf of bread, a used car, an hour of a plumber's time. Other things turn strange the moment someone sticks one on: a friendship, a vote, a child.

John Paul the Second wrote a letter marking a hundred years since Rerum Novarum, after the communist governments of Eastern Europe had fallen. It could have handed down a simple verdict on which economic system had won.
Instead it's more careful: the market is a real good, and the market has edges. Its name means the hundredth year. Today's word is Centesimus Annus.

teach.b: First, what markets do well. The letter calls the free market an efficient way to use resources and meet needs.
It praises initiative, enterprise and work, and says profit has a proper place, as a sign that a business is doing its job. Second, where markets stop.
There are many human needs, the letter says, that the market can't meet, because the people who have them have nothing to pay with.

teach.h: GOODS THAT MUST NOT BE BOUGHT.
teach.b: And some goods, by their very nature, cannot and must not be bought or sold. It leaves the list open; a verdict in court might be one, a child's care another. Profit is a sign, but not the only sign.
A business is first a community of people. Third, having and being.
The letter warns about consumerism: not the wish to live better, which it calls good, but a way of life aimed at having more rather than being more.

teach.h: NOT IN THE ABUNDANCE OF THINGS.
teach.b: Jesus puts it bluntly in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "a man's life doth not consist in the abundance of things which he possesseth." Fourth, the big question. Is a free economy the answer?
If it means freedom to work and do business, set inside a strong framework of law that serves the whole human person, yes. If it means an economy answerable to nothing but itself, no.
A market inside a moral frame, not a market as the frame.

how: Catholics draw on Centesimus Annus in business ethics, economics courses at Catholic universities and in thinking about consumer choices, and it is often read together with Rerum Novarum.

games.q: the old regimes have fallen. someone asks the pope: so is a free economy the answer?
o: yes, in every form, without conditions.
yes, if it serves the whole person inside a strong framework of law.
games.why: the letter gives a careful yes: freedom to work and do business, set inside law that serves the human person, not an economy answerable to nothing.

practice: Bring to mind the next thing you're likely to buy, groceries, a gift, something in a cart, and hold it: who made it, and were they paid fairly?
Do you need it, or does it promise to make you more than you are, and is there a way to buy it that serves people better?
No guilt needed, just attention; if you pray, ask for a free heart toward things; if you don't, simply decide what you'll do.

wordCard.voice: Centesimus Annus. The hundredth year: markets have value, and limits. This week: read the signs, development is peace, with the poor, justice is gospel, the person first, sin in systems, markets have limits. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the hundredth year, the letter's opening words.

carryVoice: Your line: markets have limits. Some goods were never for sale. That's the day.
